claims.text: Conventionally processed HfZrTiTa0.53 has a relatively homogeneous, high-strength microstructure.
HfZrTiTa0.53 currently has approximately 13.5% uniform tensile elongation.
The proposed intervention is approximately 50% cold reduction followed by annealing for a few minutes at 900–1000°C.
The annealing treatment will be performed in an inert atmosphere.
Cold reduction and short annealing will produce a controlled bimodal microstructure in HfZrTiTa0.53.
The proposed microstructure will contain ultrafine recrystallized, ductile grains interspersed with work-hardened regions.
The bimodal microstructure constitutes a dual-phase microstructure.
Recrystallized regions will accommodate additional plastic deformation through enhanced grain-boundary sliding.
Recrystallized regions will accommodate additional plastic deformation through dislocation movement.
Work-hardened regions will maintain high strength.
The engineered microstructure will delay tensile necking.
The engineered microstructure will support high impact-triggered energy release.
The treatment will increase uniform tensile elongation by approximately 15–20% relative to a 13.5% baseline.
The treatment will preserve or improve yield strength relative to untreated HfZrTiTa0.53.
The treatment will preserve or improve compressive strength relative to untreated HfZrTiTa0.53.
The treatment will preserve or improve impact-triggered energy release relative to untreated HfZrTiTa0.53.
The predictions apply from room temperature to moderately elevated temperatures at a nominal quasi-static strain rate of approximately 10^-3 s^-1.
The magnitude of the ductility improvement depends on successful and uniform formation of the bimodal microstructure.

contradictions.description: The deformation magnitude is alternately specified as 50% thickness reduction and 50% cross-sectional-area reduction; these are not generally equivalent processing conditions.

The conditions assign a quasi-static strain rate of about 10^-3 s^-1 to all mechanical tests, including impact, whereas the falsification experiment calls for impact-triggered penetration tests, which require a dynamic loading regime rather than the stated quasi-static rate.
